articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Developments in near Infra-Red Visible Ultraviolet Detectors' (Digest No.165)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Developments in near Infra-Red Visible Ultraviolet Detectors
IEE Colloquium on Developments in near Infra-Red Visible Ultraviolet Detectors
abstract: The author describes a new solid state detector which fulfils all the requirements of the ideal detector for optical radiation measurements. This 'trap' detector is shown to be spatially uniform, linear, stable and with a predictable relative spectral response so that it can be used to realise a relative spectral response scale with an uncertainty of less than 0.05%. The detector is also shown to be capable of disseminating an absolute spectral responsivity scale with an uncertainty of less than 0.02% at specific laser wavelengths and independently realising such a scale with an uncertainty of better than 0.05%.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Developments in near Infra-Red Visible Ultraviolet Detectors
abstract: Recent work on infrared detectors and systems is described. Emphasis on the development of staring array devices and the inherent systems benefits. In conventional mechanically scanned systems the stare efficiency is very low, typically less than 0.1%. However, by increasing the number of detectors on the focal plane this stare efficiency and hence the thermal resolution of the system can be improved significantly. The ideal solution would be a large two-dimensional close packed matrix of sensors, in which every pixel in the required scene is imaged onto its own corresponding detector. In addition to increasing the system performance, the mechanics of the system would be greatly simplified, and in many cases totally eliminated thus producing simple and potentially cheap and rugged imaging systems. Both cooled and uncooled devices are discussed and typical imagery demonstrated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An introduction to optical radiation detectors
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Developments in near Infra-Red Visible Ultraviolet Detectors
abstract: The author gives a general introduction to the variety of detectors available which respond to optical radiation at wavelengths ranging from 200 nm to 2.5 mu m. There are two main types of detector, thermal detectors and photon detectors. Thermal detectors convert optical power into heat and incorporate a means of sensing the resulting heat flow. Photon detectors respond to individual photons independent of their energy.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Developments in NIR detector systems (for telecommunications)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Developments in near Infra-Red Visible Ultraviolet Detectors
abstract: The NIR region is discussed from about 1 mu m to about 1.6 mu m, the spectral region which includes the most heavily used telecommunications windows and is thus covered by detector components developed for such application. The aim of the author's overview is to look at the range of detectors and detection schemes available in this window, starting with direct (amplitude) measurement, then moving on towards more advanced signal recovery methods involving coherent techniques. The availability of optical amplifiers in this window is a further inducement to broader study.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The long term stability of the response of silicon photodiodes
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Developments in near Infra-Red Visible Ultraviolet Detectors
abstract: The author presents the results of an investigation into the long term stability of the response of a number of different types of silicon photodiode. The study aimed to quantify the ageing of the spectral responsivity of silicon photodiodes and where possible identify parameters that contributed to any instability. Five types of commercially available photovoltaic silicon photodiodes were chosen and twenty diodes of each type were monitored.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
